question.subject: Mathematics
question.question_title: Five distinct straight lines pass through \(O\). Let \(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3,\alpha_4,\alpha_5\) be any selection containing exactly one angle from each pair of vertically opposite angles. What is \(\alpha_1+\alpha_2+\alpha_3+\alpha_4+\alpha_5\)?
question.explanation: Arrange the five smaller angles between successive lines on one side of \(O\) as \(\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3,\theta_4,\theta_5\). They form a straight angle, so \(\theta_1+\theta_2+\theta_3+\theta_4+\theta_5=180^\circ\). Vertically opposite angles are equal, so any one angle from each opposite pair has the same sum.

options.label: \(180^\circ\)
options.rationale: The selected angles correspond to the angles in one semicircle.

options.label: \(90^\circ\)
options.rationale: A semicircle around a point measures \(180^\circ\).

options.label: \(360^\circ\)
options.rationale: This is the sum of all angles around \(O\), not one from each opposite pair.

options.label: \(720^\circ\)
options.rationale: This exceeds the full angular measure around a point.

question.subject: Mathematics
question.question_title: Two parallel lines \(l\) and \(m\) are cut by a transversal \(t\) at \(P\) and \(Q\). Let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) be the interior angles on the same side of \(t\). Which proof correctly establishes the proposition \(\alpha+\beta=180^\circ\)?
question.explanation: An alternate interior angle \(\gamma\) equals \(\beta\) because \(l\parallel m\). The angles \(\alpha\) and \(\gamma\) form a linear pair, so their sum is \(180^\circ\). Therefore, \(\alpha+\beta=180^\circ\).

options.label: Let \(\gamma\) be the alternate interior angle to \(\beta\) at \(P\). Since \(l\parallel m\), \(\gamma=\beta\), and since \(\alpha\) and \(\gamma\) form a linear pair, \(\alpha+\gamma=180^\circ\). Hence \(\alpha+\beta=180^\circ\).
options.rationale: It combines alternate interior angle equality with the linear-pair property.

options.label: Since \(l\parallel m\), corresponding angles are supplementary, so \(\alpha+\beta=180^\circ\).
options.rationale: Corresponding angles are equal, not supplementary.

options.label: The angles \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are vertically opposite angles, so \(\alpha=\beta\).
options.rationale: They are at different intersection points and are not vertically opposite.

options.label: Alternate interior angles always form a linear pair, so \(\alpha+\beta=180^\circ\).
options.rationale: Alternate interior angles are equal, not necessarily a linear pair.

question.subject: Mathematics
question.question_title: Two chords \(AB\) and \(CD\) of a circle intersect at \(P\) inside the circle. If \(PA=4\,\mathrm{cm}\), \(PB=9\,\mathrm{cm}\), and \(PC=6\,\mathrm{cm}\), which proposition gives the length of \(PD\)?
question.explanation: For intersecting chords, \(PA\cdot PB=PC\cdot PD\). Therefore, \(4\times9=6\times PD\), so \(PD=6\,\mathrm{cm}\).

options.label: \(PD=6\,\mathrm{cm}\)
options.rationale: Intersecting chords give \(PA\cdot PB=PC\cdot PD\).

options.label: \(PD=\frac{3}{2}\,\mathrm{cm}\)
options.rationale: This reverses the product relation for the intersecting chords.

options.label: \(PD=13\,\mathrm{cm}\)
options.rationale: A sum relation is not applicable to intersecting chords.

options.label: \(PD=\frac{27}{2}\,\mathrm{cm}\)
options.rationale: This results from multiplying instead of dividing by \(PC\).

question.subject: Mathematics
question.question_title: Let \(M\) be the midpoint of \(AB\), and \(C\) be any point not on line \(AB\). Which sequence of equalities correctly proves \(CA^{2}+CB^{2}=2\left(CM^{2}+AM^{2}\right)\)?
question.explanation: Since \(M\) is the midpoint, \(AM=BM\). Also, \(\angle CMB=180^{\circ}-\angle CMA\), so the cosine terms in the two cosine-rule expansions cancel, giving \(CA^{2}+CB^{2}=2\left(CM^{2}+AM^{2}\right)\).

options.label: \(CA^{2}=CM^{2}+AM^{2}-2\,CM\cdot AM\cos\angle CMA\), \(CB^{2}=CM^{2}+AM^{2}+2\,CM\cdot AM\cos\angle CMA\), hence \(CA^{2}+CB^{2}=2\left(CM^{2}+AM^{2}\right)\)
options.rationale: The cosine terms cancel because \(AM=BM\) and \(\angle CMB\) is supplementary to \(\angle CMA\).

options.label: \(CA^{2}=CM^{2}+AM^{2}+2\,CM\cdot AM\cos\angle CMA\), \(CB^{2}=CM^{2}+AM^{2}+2\,CM\cdot AM\cos\angle CMA\)
options.rationale: Both cosine terms cannot have the same sign.

options.label: \(CA^{2}+CB^{2}=2\left(CM^{2}-AM^{2}\right)\) by applying the cosine rule
options.rationale: The squared midpoint distance contributes positively.

options.label: \(CA^{2}+CB^{2}=2\left(CM+AM\right)^{2}\) because \(M\) is the midpoint
options.rationale: Midpoint symmetry does not make the two distances equal to \(CM+AM\).

question.subject: Mathematics
question.question_title: In triangle \(ABC\), \(AD\) bisects \(\angle A\) and meets \(BC\) at \(D\). Which chain of equalities correctly proves the angle-bisector theorem \(\frac{BD}{DC}=\frac{AB}{AC}\)?
question.explanation: Triangles \(ABD\) and \(ACD\) have the same altitude from \(A\) to \(BC\), so their area ratio is \(BD/DC\). Using the area formula with common factor \(AD\), the ratio is \(AB\sin\angle BAD/(AC\sin\angle CAD)\). Since \(AD\) bisects \(\angle A\), the sine factors are equal, proving \(BD/DC=AB/AC\).

options.label: \(\frac{\mathrm{Area}(\triangle ABD)}{\mathrm{Area}(\triangle ACD)}=\frac{BD}{DC}=\frac{AB\sin\angle BAD}{AC\sin\angle CAD}=\frac{AB}{AC}\)
options.rationale: The first equality uses the common altitude, and the second uses the area formula and \(\angle BAD=\angle CAD\).

options.label: \(\frac{\mathrm{Area}(\triangle ABD)}{\mathrm{Area}(\triangle ACD)}=\frac{BD}{DC}=\frac{AC}{AB}\)
options.rationale: The side ratio is reversed.

options.label: \(\frac{\mathrm{Area}(\triangle ABD)}{\mathrm{Area}(\triangle ACD)}=\frac{AB}{AC}=\frac{\sin\angle BAD}{\sin\angle CAD}\)
options.rationale: The area ratio contains both side and sine factors before cancellation.

options.label: \(\frac{\mathrm{Area}(\triangle ABD)}{\mathrm{Area}(\triangle ACD)}=\frac{AD}{BC}\)
options.rationale: The two triangles have a common altitude, so their area ratio depends on \(BD\) and \(DC\).
